answer:
The variational method found H2's lowest energy to within 1e-12 hartree of the exact answer when I ran it on a simulator. The final measurement job on garnet:mock gave -0.163 hartree. That number is not chemistry, because the mock device returns made-up counts.

The model. I used the standard H2 STO-3G Hamiltonian at 0.735 angstrom, in its 2-qubit form (parity mapping with two-qubit reduction). The energy is a weighted sum of 5 Pauli terms: II, IZ, ZI, ZZ and XX. I used the standard published coefficients for this geometry and added the nuclear repulsion of 0.71997 hartree.

The exact answer. I diagonalized the 4x4 Hamiltonian matrix on a normal computer. The exact ground-state energy is -1.137306 hartree.

The variational loop. The circuit sets one qubit to 1, rotates the other qubit by an angle theta, and then applies a CNOT. This makes a mix of the two electron arrangements that matter for H2. I tried 73 settings of theta on a simulator and then refined the best one in 60 more steps. I kept the best setting, theta = -0.2235 rad. A perfect quantum computer would give -1.137306 hartree with this circuit, which matches the exact answer.

The final job. I submitted one job with 2 circuits and 1000 shots each to garnet:mock. Job ID: 01a16041-dbbc-775c-9d61-d914f438985c. It completed and cost 0 credits. Circuit 1 measures in the normal basis, which gives the IZ, ZI and ZZ terms. Circuit 2 rotates both qubits with Hadamard gates first, which gives the XX term. The mock device returned about half 00 and half 11 for both circuits. That pattern does not depend on the circuit, so the measured energy came out at -0.163 hartree. This is about 0.97 hartree above the exact answer.

A local test of the same two circuits on a noiseless sampler gave -1.1415 hartree. That is within about 0.004 hartree of the exact answer, and the gap comes from shot noise. On real hardware, gate and readout errors would move the result away from the exact answer, often by tens of millihartree, and you would need error mitigation to get close to chemical accuracy (1.6 millihartree).

The principle. A quantum computer prepares a trial electron state and measures its energy one Pauli term at a time. A classical optimizer adjusts the circuit settings to lower that energy. The variational principle says no trial state can go below the true ground-state energy, so the lowest value found is an upper bound that approaches the exact answer.

The script is /Users/claytonchancey/Desktop/quantum/.claude/worktrees/wf_664c303a-347-32/h2_vqe.py.
